title: Middleware, CORS and background tasks
summary: A middleware wraps every request and response (logs, timings, headers).

sections.definition: A middleware wraps every request and response (logs, timings, headers). CORS is a browser rule: it blocks responses from another origin unless the server allows it with headers; it is configured with CORSMiddleware. BackgroundTasks runs something after the response is sent, like a confirmation email.
sections.analogy: The middleware is the building's doorman: everyone goes past him on the way in and on the way out. The background task is “we'll email you the receipt”: you leave with your coffee and the email goes out afterwards.
sections.problem: Without CORS configured, your frontend on localhost:4200 cannot read the responses from the API on localhost:8000. Without background tasks, the user waits for an email to go out before seeing their order.
sections.code:example:
import time
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, Request
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:4200", "https://tienda.co"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

@app.middleware("http")
async def medir_tiempo(request: Request, call_next):
    inicio = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)        # sigue la cadena
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = f"{time.perf_counter() - inicio:.4f}"
    return response

def enviar_confirmacion(email: str, pedido_id: int) -> None:
    ...  # SMTP: lento

@app.post("/pedidos", status_code=201)
def crear_pedido(datos: PedidoCrear, tareas: BackgroundTasks, cliente: ClienteActual):
    pedido = guardar_pedido(datos, cliente)
    tareas.add_task(enviar_confirmacion, cliente.email, pedido.id)
    return pedido                               # el cliente no espera el correo
sections.bad:
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
)

Any website could make requests with your users' credentials. The CORS specification does not allow * when there are credentials.
sections.good:
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=settings.cors_origins,   # lista explícita
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
)

Explicit origins from configuration.
sections.bridge:typescript: Middleware resembles Express's (req, res, next): await call_next(request) ≈ next(). On the client side, it is the same idea as a function wrapping fetch to touch every request. And the CORS error you used to see in the browser console gets fixed here, not on the frontend (in development you also dodged it with the dev server's proxy).
sections.interview: Middleware intercepts all requests and responses; I use it for logs, metrics or headers, like a function wrapping fetch on the client, but on the server. CORS is a browser protection: I configure CORSMiddleware with an explicit list of origins, never an asterisk with credentials, knowing it does not protect against non-browser clients. For work that must not delay the response, like sending an email, I use BackgroundTasks; if it is heavy or cannot be lost, a task queue.
sections.myths:
• Believing CORS protects your API: only browsers enforce it; curl or Postman ignore it.
  • Using BackgroundTasks for heavy or critical jobs: if the process restarts, they are lost. Use a queue (Celery, ARQ, RQ).
  • Forgetting that requests with JSON or Authorization trigger an OPTIONS preflight.
  • Registering CORS after other middlewares that may respond first.

items.q: When does a task added with tareas.add_task(...) run?
items.why: The client receives the response and then the task runs.

items.q: What is the Express middleware equivalent of await call_next(request)?
items.why: Both pass the request to the next link in the chain. In FastAPI, in addition, call_next returns the response to you so you can modify it.
